sword_marker_records.content_osis: <div sID="gen7273" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="9" osisID="2Kgs.9" sID="2Kgs.9"/> <div eID="gen7273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7274" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7275" type="x-p"/> Hazael and Jehu were the men that were designed to be the instruments of God's justice in punishing and destroying the house of Ahab. Elijah was told to appoint them to this service; but, upon Ahab's humiliation, a reprieve was granted, and so it was left to Elisha to appoint them. Hazael's elevation to the throne of Syria we read of in the foregoing chapter; and we must now attend Jehu to the throne of Israel; for him that escapeth the sword of Hazael, as Joram and Ahaziah did, Jehu must slay, of which this chapter gives us an account. I. A commission is sent to Jehu by the hand of one of the prophets, to take upon him the government, and destroy the house of Ahab, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.1-2Kgs.9.10">ver. 1-10</reference>. II. Here is his speedy execution of this commission. 1. He communicates it to his captains, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.11-2Kgs.9.15">ver. 11-15</reference>. 2. He marches directly to Jezreel (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.16-2Kgs.9.20">ver. 16-20</reference>), and there dispatches (1.) Joram king of Israel, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.21-2Kgs.9.26">ver. 21-26</reference>. (2.) Ahaziah king of Judah, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.27-2Kgs.9.29">ver. 27-29</reference>. (3.) Jezebel, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.30-2Kgs.9.37">ver. 30-37</reference>.

(<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 884.)</title> <div sID="gen7276" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And Elisha the prophet called one of the children of the prophets, and said unto him, Gird up thy loins, and take this box of oil in thine hand, and go to Ramoth-gilead: <hi type="super">2</hi> And when thou comest thither, look out there Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi, and go in, and make him arise up from among his brethren, and carry him to an inner chamber; <hi type="super">3</hi> Then take the box of oil, and pour <hi type="italic">it</hi> on his head, and say, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , I have anointed thee king over Israel. Then open the door, and flee, and tarry not. <hi type="super">4</hi> So the young man, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the young man the prophet, went to Ramoth-gilead. <hi type="super">5</hi> And when he came, behold, the captains of the host <hi type="italic">were</hi> sitting; and he said, I have an errand to thee, O captain. And Jehu said, Unto which of all us? And he said, To thee, O captain. <hi type="super">6</hi> And he arose, and went into the house; and he poured the oil on his head, and said unto him, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel, I have anointed thee king over the people of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">even</hi> over Israel. <hi type="super">7</hi> And thou shalt smite the house of Ahab thy master, that I may avenge the blood of my servants the prophets, and the blood of all the servants of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , at the hand of Jezebel. <hi type="super">8</hi> For the whole house of Ahab shall perish: and I will cut off from Ahab him that pisseth against the wall, and him that is shut up and left in Israel: <hi type="super">9</hi> And I will make the house of Ahab like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and like the house of Baasha the son of Ahijah: <hi type="super">10</hi> And the dogs shall eat Jezebel in the portion of Jezreel, and <hi type="italic">there shall be</hi> none to bury <hi type="italic">her.</hi> And he opened the door, and fled. <div eID="gen7276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7277" type="x-p"/> We have here the anointing of Jehu to be king, who was, at this time, a commander (probably commander-in-chief) of the forces employed at Ramoth-Gilead, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.14">v. 14</reference>. There he was fighting for the king his master, but received orders from a higher king to fight against him. It does not appear that Jehu aimed at the government, or that he ever thought of it, but the commission given him was a perfect surprise to him. Some think that he had been anointed before by Elijah, whom God ordered to do it, but privately, and with an intimation that he must not act till further orders, as Samuel anointed David long before he was to come to the throne: but that it not at all probable, for then we must suppose Elijah had anointed Hazael too. No, when God bade him do these things he bade him anoint Elisha to <hi type="italic">be prophet in his room,</hi> to do them when he was gone, as God should direct him. Here is, <div eID="gen7277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7278" type="x-p"/> I. The commission sent. <div eID="gen7278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7279" type="x-p"/> 1. Elisha did not go himself to anoint Jehu, because he was old and unfit for such a journey and so well known that he could not do it privately, could not go and come without observation; therefore he sends <hi type="italic">one of the sons of the prophets</hi> to do it, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.1">v. 1</reference>. They not only reverences him as their father (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.2.15">ch. ii. 15</reference>), but observed and obeyed him as their father. This service of anointing Jehu, (1.) Had danger in it (<reference osisRef="1Sam.16.2">1 Sam. xvi. 2</reference>), and therefore it was not fit that Elisha should expose himself, but one of the sons of the prophets, whose life was of less value, and who could do it with less danger. (2.) It required labour and was therefore fitter for a young man in his full strength. Let youth work and age direct. (3.) Yet it was an honourable piece of service, to anoint a king, and he that did it might hope to be preferred for it afterwards, and therefore, for the encouragement of the young prophets, Elisha employed one of them: he would not engross all the honours to himself, nor grudge the young prophets a share in them. <div eID="gen7279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7280" type="x-p"/> 2. When he sent him, (1.) He put the oil into his hand with which he must anoint Jehu: <hi type="italic">Take this box of oil</hi> Solomon was anointed with <hi type="italic">oil out of the tabernacle,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.1.39">1 Kings i. 39</reference>. That could not now be had, but oil from a prophet's hand was equivalent to oil out of God's house. Probably it was not the constant practice to anoint kings, but upon the disturbance of the succession, as in the case of Solomon, or the interruption of it, as in the case of Joash (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.11.12">ch. xi. 12</reference>), or the translation of the government to a new family, as here and in the case of David; yet it might be used generally, though the scripture does not mention it. (2.) He put <hi type="italic">the words into his mouth</hi> which he must say (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.3">v. 3</reference>)—<hi type="italic">I have anointed thee king,</hi> and, no doubt, told him all the rest that he said, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.7-2Kgs.9.10">v. 7-10</reference>. Those whom God sends on his errands shall not go without full instructions. (3.) He also ordered him, [1.] To do it privately, to single out Jehu from the rest of the captains and anoint him <hi type="italic">in an inner chamber</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.2">v. 2</reference>), that Jehu's confidence in his commission might be tried, when he had no witness to attest it. His being suddenly animated for the service would be proof sufficient of his being anointed to it. There needed no other proof. The thing signified was the best evidence of the sign. [2.] To do it expeditiously. When he went about it he must <hi type="italic">gird up his loins;</hi> when he had done it he must <hi type="italic">flee and not tarry</hi> for a fee, or a treat, or to see what Jehu would do. It becomes the sons of the prophets to be quick and lively at their work, to go about it and go through it as men that hate sauntering and trifling. They should be as angels that fly swiftly. <div eID="gen7280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7281" type="x-p"/> II. The commission delivered. The young prophet did his business with despatch, was at Ramoth-Gilead presently, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.4">v. 4</reference>. There he found the general officers sitting together, either at dinner or in a council of war, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.5">v. 5</reference>. When the prophet had him alone he anointed him, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.6">v. 6</reference>. The anointing of the Spirit is a hidden thing, that new name which none knows but those that have it. Herewith, <div eID="gen7281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7282" type="x-p"/> 1. He invests him with the royal dignity: <hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord God of Israel,</hi> whose messenger I am, in his name <hi type="italic">I have anointed thee king over the people of the Lord.</hi> He gives him an incontestable title, but reminds him that he was made king, (1.) <hi type="italic">By the God of Israel;</hi> from him he must see his power derived (for by him kings reign), for he must use it, and to him he must be accountable. Magistrates are the ministers of God, and must therefore act in dependence upon him and with an entire devotedness to him and to his glory. (2.) <hi type="italic">Over the Israel of God.</hi> Though the people of Israel were wretchedly corrupted, and had forfeited all the honour of relationship to God, yet they are here called the <hi type="italic">people of the Lord,</hi> for he had a right to them and had not yet given them a bill of divorce. He instructs him in his present service, which was to destroy all the house of Ahab (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.7">v. 7</reference>), not that he might clear his own way to the throne, and secure to himself the possession of it, but that he might execute the judgments of God upon that guilty and obnoxious family. But thou art under higher obligations to thy Master in heaven than to thy master Ahab. He has determined that <hi type="italic">the whole house of Ahab shall perish,</hi> and <hi type="italic">by thy hand;</hi> fear not: has not he commanded thee? Fear not sin; his command will justify thee and bear thee out: fear not danger; his command will secure and prosper thee." The commission delivered. The young prophet did his business with despatch, was at Ramoth-Gilead presently, v. 4 . There he found the general officers sitting together, either at dinner or in a council of war, v. 5 . With the assurance that became a messenger from God, notwithstanding the meanness of his appearance, he called Jehu out from the rest, not waiting his leisure, or begging his pardon for disturbing him, but as one having authority: I have an errand to thee, O captain. Magistrates are the ministers of God, and must therefore act in dependence upon him and with an entire devotedness to him and to his glory. (2.) Over the Israel of God. Though the people of Israel were wretchedly corrupted, and had forfeited all the honour of relationship to God, yet they are here called the people of the Lord, for he had a right to them and had not yet given them a bill of divorce. Jehu must look upon the people he was made king of as the people of the Lord, not as his vassals, but God's freemen, his sons, his first-born, not to be abused or tyrannized over, God's people, and therefore to be ruled for him, and according to his laws. 2. He calls Ahab his master, that the relation might be no objection. "He was thy master, and to lift up thy hand against his son and successor would be not only base ingratitude, but treason, rebellion, and all that is bad, if thou hadst not an immediate command from God to do it. He has determined that the whole house of Ahab shall perish, and by thy hand; fear not: has not he commanded thee? Fear not sin; his command will justify thee and bear thee out: fear not danger; his command will secure and prosper thee." That he might intelligently, and in a right manner, do this great execution on the house of Ahab, he tells him, (1.) What was their crime, what the ground of the controversy, and wherefore God had quarrel with them, that he might have an eye to that which God had an eye to, and that was the blood of God's servants, the prophets and others, faithful worshippers, which they had shed, and which must now be required at the hand of Jezebel. That they were idolaters was bad enough, and merited all that was brought upon them; yet that is not mentioned here, but the controversy God has with them is for their being persecutors, not so much their throwing down God's altars as their slaying his prophets with the sword. Nothing fills the measure of the iniquity of any prince or people as this does nor brings a surer or a sorer ruin. This was the sin that brought on Jerusalem its first destruction ( 2 Chron. xxxvi. 16 ) and its final one, Matt. xxiii. 37, 38 . Jezebel's whoredoms and witchcrafts were not so provoking as her persecuting the prophets, killing some and driving the rest into corners and caves, 1 Kings xviii. 4 . (2.) What was their doom. They were sentenced to utter destruction; not to be corrected, but to be cut off and rooted out. This Jehu must know, that his eye might not spare for pity, favour, or affection. A pattern is given him of the destruction intended, in the destruction of the families of Jeroboam and Baasha ( v. 9 ), and he is particularly directed to throw Jezebel to the dogs, v. 10 . The prophet, having done this errand, made the best of his way home again, and left Jehu alone to consider what he had to do and beg direction from God.

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen7289" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Jehu's Approach to Jezreel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 884.)</title> <div sID="gen7290" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> So Jehu rode in a chariot, and went to Jezreel; for Joram lay there. And Ahaziah king of Judah was come down to see Joram. <hi type="super">17</hi> And there stood a watchman on the tower in Jezreel, and he spied the company of Jehu as he came, and said, I see a company. And Joram said, Take a horseman, and send to meet them, and let him say, <hi type="italic">Is it</hi> peace? <hi type="super">18</hi> So there went one on horseback to meet him, and said, Thus saith the king, <hi type="italic">Is it</hi> peace? And Jehu said, What hast thou to do with peace? turn thee behind me. And the watchman told, saying, The messenger came to them, but he cometh not again. <hi type="super">19</hi> Then he sent out a second on horseback, which came to them, and said, Thus saith the king, <hi type="italic">Is it</hi> peace? And Jehu answered, What hast thou to do with peace? turn thee behind me. <hi type="super">20</hi> And the watchman told, saying, He came even unto them, and cometh not again: and the driving <hi type="italic">is</hi> like the driving of Jehu the son of Nimshi; for he driveth furiously. <hi type="super">21</hi> And Joram said, Make ready. And his chariot was made ready. And Joram king of Israel and Ahaziah king of Judah went out, each in his chariot, and they went out against Jehu, and met him in the portion of Naboth the Jezreelite. <hi type="super">22</hi> And it came to pass, when Joram saw Jehu, that he said, <hi type="italic">Is it</hi> peace, Jehu? And he answered, What peace, so long as the whoredoms of thy mother Jezebel and her witchcrafts <hi type="italic">are so</hi> many? <hi type="super">23</hi> And Joram turned his hands, and fled, and said to Ahaziah, <hi type="italic">There is</hi> treachery, O Ahaziah. <hi type="super">24</hi> And Jehu drew a bow with his full strength, and smote Jehoram between his arms, and the arrow went out at his heart, and he sunk down in his chariot. <hi type="super">25</hi> Then said <hi type="italic">Jehu</hi> to Bidkar his captain, Take up, <hi type="italic">and</hi> cast him in the portion of the field of Naboth the Jezreelite: for remember how that, when I and thou rode together after Ahab his father, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> laid this burden upon him; <hi type="super">26</hi> Surely I have seen yesterday the blood of Naboth, and the blood of his sons, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and I will requite thee in this plat, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . Now therefore take <hi type="italic">and</hi> cast him into the plat <hi type="italic">of ground,</hi> according to the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">27</hi> But when Ahaziah the king of Judah saw <hi type="italic">this,</hi> he fled by the way of the garden house. And Jehu followed after him, and said, Smite him also in the chariot. <hi type="italic">And they did so</hi> at the going up to Gur, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> by Ibleam. And he fled to Megiddo, and died there. <hi type="super">28</hi> And his servants carried him in a chariot to Jerusalem, and buried him in his sepulchre with his fathers in the city of David. <hi type="super">29</hi> And in the eleventh year of Joram the son of Ahab began Ahaziah to reign over Judah. <div eID="gen7290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7291" type="x-p"/> From Ramoth-Gilead to Jezreel was more than one day's march; about the mid-way between them the river Jordan must be crossed. We may suppose Jehu to have marched with all possible expedition, and to have taken the utmost precaution to prevent the tidings from getting to Jezreel before him; and, at length, we have him within sight first, and then within reach, of the devoted king. <div eID="gen7291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7292" type="x-p"/> I. Joram's watchman discovers him first at a distance, him and his retinue, and gives notice to the king of the approach of a company, whether of friends or foes he cannot tell. But the king (impatient to know what is the matter, and perhaps jealous that the Syrians, who had wounded him, had traced him by the blood to his own palace, and were coming to seize him) sent first one messenger, and then another, to bring him intelligence, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.17-2Kgs.9.19">v. 17-19</reference>. He had scarcely recovered from the fright he was put into in the battle, and his guilty conscience put him into a continual terror. Each messenger asked the same question: "<hi type="italic">Is it peace?</hi> are you for us or for our adversaries? Do you bring good tidings or bad?" Each had the same answer: <hi type="italic">What hast thou to do with peace? Turn thee behind me,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.18-2Kgs.9.19">v. 18, 19</reference>. As if he had said, "It is not to thee, but to him that sent thee, that I will give answer; for thy part, if thou consult thy own safety, <hi type="italic">turn thee behind me,</hi> and enlist thyself among my followers." The watchman gave notice that the messengers were taken prisoners, and at length observed that the leader of this troop drove like Jehu, who it seems was noted for driving furiously, thereby discovering himself to be a man of a hot eager spirit, intent upon his business, and pushing forward with all his might. A man of such a violent temper was fittest for the service to which Jehu was designated. The wisdom of God is seen in the choice of proper instruments to be employed in his work. But it is not much for any man's reputation to be known by his fury. He that has rule over his own spirit is better than the mighty. The Chaldee paraphrase gives this a contrary sense: <hi type="italic">The leading is like that of Jehu, for he leads quietly.</hi> And, it should seem, he did not come up very fast, for then there would not have been time for all this that passed. And some think he chose to march slowly, that he might give Joram time to come out to him, and so dispatch him before he entered the city. <div eID="gen7292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7293" type="x-p"/> II. Joram himself goes out to meet him, and takes Ahaziah king of Judah along with him, neither of them equipped for war, as not expecting an enemy, but in haste to have their curiosity satisfied. How strangely has Providence sometimes ordered it, that men have been in haste to meet their ruin when their day has come to fall. <div eID="gen7293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7294" type="x-p"/> 1. The place where Joram met Jehu was ominous: <hi type="italic">In the portion of Naboth the Jezreelite,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.21">v. 21</reference>. The very sight of that ground was enough to make Joram tremble and Jehu triumph; for Joram had the guilt of Naboth's blood fighting against him and Jehu had the force of Elijah's curse fighting for him. The circumstances of events are sometimes so ordered by divine Providence as to make the punishment answer to the sin as face answers to face in a glass. <div eID="gen7294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7295" type="x-p"/> 2. Joram's demand was still the same: "<hi type="italic">Is it peace, Jehu?</hi> Is all well? Dost thou come home thus flying from the Syrians or more than a conqueror over them?" It seems, he looked for peace, and could not entertain any other thought. Note, It is very common for great sinners, even when they are upon the brink of ruin, to flatter themselves with an opinion that all is well with them, and to cry peace to themselves. <div eID="gen7295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7296" type="x-p"/> 3. Jehu's reply was very startling. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 884.)</title> <div sID="gen7298" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">30</hi> And when Jehu was come to Jezreel, Jezebel heard <hi type="italic">of it;</hi> and she painted her face, and tired her head, and looked out at a window. <hi type="super">31</hi> And as Jehu entered in at the gate, she said, <hi type="italic">Had</hi> Zimri peace, who slew his master? <hi type="super">32</hi> And he lifted up his face to the window, and said, Who <hi type="italic">is</hi> on my side? who? And there looked out to him two <hi type="italic">or</hi> three eunuchs. <hi type="super">33</hi> And he said, Throw her down. So they threw her down: and <hi type="italic">some</hi> of her blood was sprinkled on the wall, and on the horses: and he trode her under foot. <hi type="super">34</hi> And when he was come in, he did eat and drink, and said, Go, see now this cursed <hi type="italic">woman,</hi> and bury her: for she <hi type="italic">is</hi> a king's daughter. <hi type="super">35</hi> And they went to bury her: but they found no more of her than the skull, and the feet, and the palms of <hi type="italic">her</hi> hands. <hi type="super">36</hi> Wherefore they came again, and told him. And he said, This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , which he spake by his servant Elijah the Tishbite, saying, In the portion of Jezreel shall dogs eat the flesh of Jezebel: <hi type="super">37</hi> And the carcase of Jezebel shall be as dung upon the face of the field in the portion of Jezreel; <hi type="italic">so</hi> that they shall not say, This <hi type="italic">is</hi> Jezebel. <div eID="gen7298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7299" type="x-p"/> The greatest delinquent in the house of Ahab was Jezebel: it was she that introduced Baal, slew the Lord's prophets, contrived the murder of Naboth, stirred up her husband first, and then her sons, to do wickedly; a <hi type="italic">cursed woman</hi> she is here called (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.34">v. 34</reference>), a curse to the country, and whom all that wished well to their country had a curse for. Three reigns her reign had lasted, but now, at length, her day had come to fall. We read of a false prophetess in the church of Thyatira that is compared to Jezebel, and called by her name (<reference osisRef="Rev.2.20">Rev. ii. 20</reference>), her wickedness the same, seducing God's servants to idolatry, a long <hi type="italic">space given her to repent</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.21">v. 21</reference>) as to Jezebel, and a fearful ruin brought upon her at last (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.22-2Kgs.9.23">v. 22, 23</reference>), as here upon Jezebel. So that Jezebel's destruction may be looked upon as typical of the destruction of idolaters and persecutors, especially that great whore, that mother of harlots, that hath made herself <hi type="italic">drunk with the blood of saints</hi> and the nations <hi type="italic">drunk with the wine of her fornications,</hi> when God shall put it into the heart of the kings of the earth to hate her, <reference osisRef="Rev.17.5-Rev.17.6">Rev. xvii. 5, 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.17.16">16</reference>. Now here we have, <div eID="gen7299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7300" type="x-p"/> I. Jezebel daring the judgment. She heard that Jehu had slain her son, and slain him for her whoredoms and witchcrafts, and thrown his dead body into the portion of Naboth, according to the word of the Lord, and that he was now coming to Jezreel, where she could not but expect herself to fall next a sacrifice to his revenging sword. Now see how she meets her fate; she posted herself in a window at the entering of the gate, to affront Jehu and set him at defiance. 1. Instead of hiding herself, as one afraid of divine vengeance, she exposed herself to it and scorned to flee, mocked at fear and was not affrighted. See how a heart hardened against God will brave it out to the last, <hi type="italic">run upon him, even upon his neck,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.15.26">Job xv. 26</reference>. But never did any thus harden their hearts against him and prosper. 2. Instead of humbling herself, and putting herself into close mourning for her son, she <hi type="italic">painted her face, and tired her head,</hi> that she might appear like herself, that is (as she thought), great and majestic, hoping thereby to daunt Jehu, to put him out of countenance, and to stop his career. <hi type="italic">The Lord God called to baldness and girding with sackcloth,</hi> but behold painting and dressing, walking contrary to God, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.12-Isa.22.13">Isa. xxii. 12, 13</reference>. There is not a surer presage of ruin than an unhumbled heart under humbling providences. Let painted faces look in Jezebel's glass, and see how they like themselves. 3.
